title: Primary Function of the Robot Arm
learningObjectives: Identify the arm's structural role in the manipulator.
student: State the primary structural function of the robot arm.
instructor: The arm positions the gripper and transfers payload and self-weight loads to the robot body through pin A and hydraulic cylinder BD.

title: External Loads on Arm ABC
learningObjectives: Identify all external actions on the isolated arm.
student: Identify all external loads acting directly on arm ABC.
instructor: The arm carries uniform downward load w, concentrated downward payload P at C, pin reactions Ax and Ay, and the force exerted by cylinder BD at B.

title: Support Idealizations at A and B
learningObjectives: Describe the support forces admitted by each idealization.
student: Describe the idealizations at pin A and cylinder attachment B.
instructor: A is a frictionless pin with unknown reactions Ax and Ay and no reaction moment. BD is a two-force member, so its force at B acts along the cylinder axis.

title: Load Path to the Floor
learningObjectives: Trace load transfer through the manipulator.
student: Trace the load path from the payload and arm weight to the floor.
instructor: Payload, gripper, and arm weight transfer through arm ABC to pin A and cylinder BD, then through the robot body and base to the floor.

title: Central Structural Response
learningObjectives: Identify the internal resultants central to the assignment.
student: Which structural responses are the central focus of this problem, and why?
instructor: Internal vertical shear and bending moment are central because the transverse distributed and concentrated loads create bending demand along the arm.

title: Parameters Controlling the Diagrams
learningObjectives: Identify inputs controlling shear and moment.
student: Identify the variables that control the shear-force and bending-moment diagrams.
instructor: The governing inputs are overhang a, distance A-to-B b, distance B-to-C L, uniform weight w, payload P, and cylinder-force direction θ.

title: Two-Force-Member Interpretation
learningObjectives: Explain why the cylinder has one force unknown.
student: Explain why only one unknown magnitude is required for the force in cylinder BD.
instructor: An ideal two-force member carries only an axial force along the line joining its end pins. Its direction is known, so only the magnitude is unknown.

title: Student-Generated Beam Idealization
learningObjectives: Translate the manipulator into a beam and free-body diagram.
student: Before using the reference figure, replace the manipulator with a horizontal beam model. Show the left free tip, pin A, cylinder attachment B, end C, uniform load w, payload P, and cylinder force along BD.
instructor: A valid idealization places pin A a distance a from the left free tip, B another distance b to the right, and C a distance L beyond B. It includes Ax, Ay, the inclined cylinder force, full-length uniform load, and end payload.
gradingNotes: Students should attempt the beam FBD before seeing the instructor reference figure.

title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State assumptions supporting the beam analysis.
student: State the assumptions used in the simplified analysis.
instructor: Assume a straight initially horizontal arm, static loading, small deformation, uniform w over the full arm-and-gripper length, a frictionless pin at A, an ideal two-force cylinder, and negligible joint and gripper dimensions. Exclude dynamics, fatigue, and local connection effects.

title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Plan the equilibrium and internal-loading analysis.
student: List the mechanics steps needed before drawing the diagrams.
instructor: Replace the distributed load by its resultant for whole-arm equilibrium; solve the cylinder force and pin reactions; define beam coordinate s; derive piecewise V(s) and M(s); plot jumps and slopes; and compare all region boundaries and zero-shear locations for the absolute maximum moment.

title: Beam Boundary Conditions
learningObjectives: Identify support restrictions and reaction components.
student: Identify the kinematic restrictions and reaction components at A and B.
instructor: Pin A prevents horizontal and vertical translation but permits arm rotation, producing Ax and Ay. Cylinder BD applies one axial force at B along its assigned direction.

title: Equivalent Uniform-Load Resultant
learningObjectives: Replace a uniform load with an equivalent resultant.
student: Replace the uniform load by an equivalent resultant for whole-arm equilibrium. Give its magnitude and location relative to pin A.
instructor: The loaded length is {{robot_total_length_in}} in. The resultant is W = w(a + b + L) = {{robot_W_lb}} lb and acts {{robot_xW_in}} in to the right of A.

title: Hydraulic-Cylinder Force
learningObjectives: Solve the two-force-member load from moment equilibrium.
student: Use moment equilibrium about A to determine the hydraulic-cylinder force. State whether BD is in tension or compression.
instructor:
ΣMA = 0 gives Byb - W xW - P(b + L) = 0, so By = {{robot_By_lb}} lb.

FBD = By/sinθ = {{robot_F_BD_lb}} lb. The assigned force direction makes the cylinder a {{robot_cylinder_state}} member.

title: Pin Reactions at A
learningObjectives: Calculate pin reaction components and directions.
student: Use force equilibrium to determine Ax and Ay. Report magnitudes and directions.
instructor:
The cylinder horizontal component is Bx = {{robot_Bx_lb}} lb. Therefore Ax = {{robot_Ax_signed_lb}} lb, or {{robot_Ax_abs_lb}} lb {{robot_Ax_direction}}.

Ay = W + P - By = {{robot_Ay_signed_lb}} lb, or {{robot_Ay_abs_lb}} lb {{robot_Ay_direction}}.

title: Beam Coordinate and Piecewise Regions
learningObjectives: Partition the beam for internal-resultant equations.
student: Let s be measured from the left free tip. Identify the regions needed for piecewise shear and moment equations.
instructor: Region 1 is 0 ≤ s ≤ a; Region 2 is a ≤ s ≤ a + b; and Region 3 is a + b ≤ s ≤ a + b + L. Concentrated-force jumps occur at A, B, and C.

title: Piecewise Shear-Force Functions
learningObjectives: Derive vertical shear in each beam region.
student: Using upward force as positive, derive V(s) in each region.
instructor: Using signed reactions, V1 = -ws; V2 = -ws + Ay; and V3 = -ws + Ay + By. At C, downward payload P causes the final jump to zero.

title: Piecewise Bending-Moment Functions
learningObjectives: Derive bending moment in each beam region.
student: Derive M(s) in each region using M(0) = 0.
instructor: M1 = -ws2/2; M2 = -ws2/2 + Ay(s - a); and M3 = -ws2/2 + Ay(s - a) + By[s - (a + b)].

title: Shear and Moment Diagram Ordinates
learningObjectives: Construct and label shear and moment diagrams.
student: Draw the shear-force and bending-moment diagrams and label the key ordinates at the free tip, A, B, and C.
instructor:
Shear values are: left tip {{robot_V_left_lb}} lb; A- {{robot_V_A_minus_lb}} lb; A+ {{robot_V_A_plus_lb}} lb; B- {{robot_V_B_minus_lb}} lb; B+ {{robot_V_B_plus_lb}} lb; C- {{robot_V_C_minus_lb}} lb; and C+ {{robot_V_C_plus_lb}} lb.

The moment diagram is continuous, with MA = {{robot_M_A_lbin}} lb·in, MB = {{robot_M_B_lbin}} lb·in, and MC = {{robot_M_C_lbin}} lb·in.

title: Absolute Maximum Bending Moment
learningObjectives: Locate and quantify the absolute maximum bending moment.
student: Determine the absolute maximum bending moment and its location. Check all beam-region boundaries and any interior locations where shear is zero.
instructor: The governing signed moment is {{robot_M_signed_max_lbin}} lb·in at {{robot_M_location}}. Therefore |M|max = {{robot_M_abs_max_lbin}} lb·in = {{robot_M_abs_max_lbft}} lb·ft.

title: Engineering Assessment
learningObjectives: Recommend the first stress-check location and a demand-reduction strategy.
student: Identify the arm section that should be checked first in a subsequent bending-stress analysis and recommend one change that would reduce demand.
instructor:
{{robot_recommendation}}

Detailed design must also evaluate axial force, bending stress and deflection, actuator capacity, pins and connections, local stress concentrations, fatigue, dynamics, stability, controls, manufacturing constraints, and safety factors.
